scenes.vo: This is a school paddle. In seventeen states, it is still legal. Whether it stays legal in your district is not decided in a state capitol. It is decided by a local school board. This film is for them.

screen.a local school board: Decided by the local school board.

scenes.vo: Last school year, American public schools reported corporal punishment of nineteen thousand eight hundred fifty-one students. That is not a count of incidents. It is a count of children. Not in nineteen seventy-four. Last year.

Nineteen thousand eight hundred fifty-one students. Twenty-eight thousand three hundred ten separate instances, which means many of them were struck more than once. In eight hundred thirty-two districts.

The federal government defines it in plain words. Paddling, spanking, or other forms of physical punishment imposed on a child. In the seventeen states that allow it, the law does not require it. It does not recommend it. It permits it, if a local school board says so. And the same board can say no.

fig.eyebrow: U.S. Department of Education · Civil Rights Data Collection
fig.quote: paddling, spanking, or other forms of physical punishment imposed on a child.
fig.sub: In every one of the seventeen states, the decision sits with the local board.

scenes.vo: Take two girls. Same town, same grade, same kind of family, same desk by the window. Call them Ava and Emma. On a Friday in September, each of them does the same thing. She shoves a classmate who took her seat. Two schools. Two policies.

Ava's school permits corporal punishment. She is sent to the office, told to bend over a chair, and struck with a wooden board. It is over in a minute. Emma's school prohibits it. She is sent to the office too. Her teacher calls home. She loses recess for a week, and she practices, with an adult, what to do the next time someone takes her seat. It takes a month.

Here is what the research says happens next. Across twenty-one studies of sixty-seven thousand children, girls like Ava are more likely to hit someone again, more likely to be anxious or depressed, and more likely to fall behind in school. Followed into their twenties, they had lower grades, more symptoms of depression, and were more likely to say they would hit their own children one day. And the one thing the paddle was for? Across seventy-five studies, it did not even reliably stop the behavior in the moment. Emma's school used the approach the research does support. Taught expectations. A consequence that fits. Practice. Across fifty-four controlled studies, that is what improved behavior and grades. This is why the people who study children for a living have all said the same thing.

left: More likely to hit her own children

scenes.sources: Visser et al. 2022 (21 studies, 67,400 children); Gershoff, Sattler and Holden 2019; Gershoff and Grogan-Kaylor 2016 (75 studies); Korpershoek et al. 2016 (54 studies)

scenes.vo: And it is already leaving. In twenty seventeen, American districts reported sixty-nine thousand four hundred ninety-two students paddled. Four years later, twenty-four thousand five hundred thirty-four. Last year, nineteen thousand eight hundred fifty-one. Down seventy-one percent in six years, mostly with no change in the law. Principals and boards are stopping on their own, one building at a time.

fig.note: in six years.|Mostly with no change in the law.

scenes.vo: Who is it still landing on? Of every hundred students paddled in America, eighty-one are boys. Seventeen have a disability. The United States Secretary of Education told every governor that Black students are more than twice as likely to be paddled as white students, and Black girls four times as likely as white girls.

scenes.vo: For the adult holding the paddle, the law offers one shield. The force has to be reasonable. Not excessive. Necessary. Those words are decided afterward, by someone else. And reasonable is no longer measured against what a town is used to. It is measured against the evidence. In twenty sixteen, seventy-nine organizations signed one letter asking every school in America to stop. The American Academy of Pediatrics. The American Psychological Association. The National Education Association. The American Federation of Teachers. The national association of school principals. The school psychologists. The National PTA. The NAACP. The ACLU. In twenty twenty-three the pediatricians said it again, on their own. And the Secretary of Education asked every state to end it.

rows: Protection runs only to force a court later agrees was reasonable, and only where the board's own policy was followed
No state's protection reaches excessive force: "reasonable but not excessive force" is the common-law rule in every state
Only the force an adult "reasonably believes to be necessary." Restatement (Second) of Torts §147(2); Ingraham v. Wright, 1977

scenes.vo: So the questions a board should be ready for are simple ones. If it does not work, and it makes the behavior worse, how do we justify it? Why are we doing something we know to be harmful? And if we are not using it anyway, why would we object to saying so in writing? More than eleven hundred school boards in those seventeen states have already answered. They did not wait for the legislature. They looked at the evidence, and they changed a line.

scenes.vo: Here is one of those policies, in full. The Board prohibits the use of corporal punishment in the District. That is the whole policy. One sentence, in a policy code every board already has.

fig.eyebrow: One board's policy, word for word

scenes.vo: Across those states, more than eight hundred districts we have checked still allow it on paper, and did not use it once last year. Their principals have already decided. The policy has not caught up. For those boards, nothing changes on Monday morning except the risk. Leadership on a school board is not a poll of what some parents prefer. It is looking at the outcomes, and acting on them.

scenes.vo: School is where we ask students to do their best, and where we show them what leadership looks like: look at the facts, and change course when the facts say to. Find your district's policy, in its own words, at earthpilot dot org slash kids. Bring the sentence to your board. The Safe Schools Project.
